<h1 id="Statistics-Walkthrough-with-Python">Statistics Walkthrough with Python¶</h1><p>This notebook performs exploratory data analysis, hypothesis testing, and regression modeling on three datasets from the repository data/ folder. Analyses use pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, seaborn, and matplotlib.</p> <p>Reproducibility: A fixed random seed (RANDOM_SEED = 42) is set wherever simulated or resampled quantities appear.</p>
In [1]:
# Global imports and reproducibility settings
import warnings
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.anova import anova_lm
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import het_breuschpagan
from statsmodels.stats.multicomp import pairwise_tukeyhsd

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=FutureWarning)

RANDOM_SEED = 42
np.random.seed(RANDOM_SEED)

# Resolve data directory relative to this notebook (ai/ -> ../data/)
DATA_DIR = Path("..").resolve() / "data"

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="notebook")
plt.rcParams["figure.figsize"] = (8, 5)

print(f"Data directory: {DATA_DIR}")

<hr /> <h2 id="Part-1:-Brain-Size-and-Intelligence-(brain_size.csv)">Part 1: Brain Size and Intelligence (brain_size.csv)¶</h2><p>Research questions</p>
  • What variables are recorded, and what do their distributions look like?
  • Do males and females differ on IQ-related measures or brain volume (MRI count)?
  • After controlling for gender, is full-scale IQ (FSIQ) associated with MRI_Count?
<p>Selected tests and rationale</p> <thead> <th>Analysis</th> <th>Test</th> <th>Why</th> </thead> <tbody> </tbody> <tbody></tbody>
Gender comparisons Welch's two-sample t-test (primary) Compares independent group means; Welch correction handles unequal variances with small n
Non-parametric backup Mann–Whitney U Robust alternative if normality is questionable in small samples
IQ ~ brain volume Multiple linear regression (OLS) Estimates adjusted association while controlling for gender
Model assumptions Residual plots, Q–Q plot, Breusch–Pagan Visual and formal checks for linearity, normality, and homoscedasticity

def compare_two_groups(data, value_col, group_col, g1, g2):
    """
    Compare two independent groups using Welch's t-test and Mann-Whitney U.

    Welch's t-test does not assume equal variances — appropriate for small samples.
    Mann-Whitney U tests whether one group tends to have larger values (non-parametric).
    """
    x = data.loc[data[group_col] == g1, value_col].dropna()
    y = data.loc[data[group_col] == g2, value_col].dropna()

    t_stat, t_p = stats.ttest_ind(x, y, equal_var=False)  # Welch's t-test
    u_stat, u_p = stats.mannwhitneyu(x, y, alternative="two-sided")

    # Levene's test informs whether variance differs markedly between groups
    lev_stat, lev_p = stats.levene(x, y)

    return {
        "variable": value_col,
        f"{g1}_mean": x.mean(),
        f"{g2}_mean": y.mean(),
        "mean_diff": x.mean() - y.mean(),
        "welch_t_p": t_p,
        "mannwhitney_p": u_p,
        "levene_p": lev_p,
        "n1": len(x),
        "n2": len(y),
    }


gender_tests = [
    compare_two_groups(brain, col, "Gender", "Male", "Female")
    for col in iq_cols
]
gender_results = pd.DataFrame(gender_tests)

print("Gender comparison results (Male minus Female):")
display(gender_results.round(4))

print(
    "\nInterpretation: A small Welch p-value suggests a statistically significant "
    "difference in group means. Compare with Mann-Whitney p-values; agreement supports "
    "the finding regardless of normality assumptions."
)

<h3 id="1.4-Linear-Regression:-FSIQ-~-MRI_Count-+-Gender">1.4 Linear Regression: FSIQ ~ MRI_Count + Gender¶</h3>
In [13]:
# Complete-case subset for regression (listwise deletion of rows with any missing predictor/outcome)
brain_reg = brain.dropna(subset=["FSIQ", "MRI_Count", "Gender"]).copy()
brain_reg["Gender"] = pd.Categorical(brain_reg["Gender"])

print(f"Regression sample size: {len(brain_reg)} observations")

# OLS with formula interface: Gender is included as a categorical predictor
brain_model = smf.ols("FSIQ ~ MRI_Count + C(Gender)", data=brain_reg).fit()
print(brain_model.summary())

<h3 id="1.5-Regression-Assumption-Checks">1.5 Regression Assumption Checks¶</h3>
In [16]:
fitted = brain_model.fittedvalues
residuals = brain_model.resid

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4))

# Residuals vs fitted: should show no curved pattern (linearity + homoscedasticity)
axes[0].scatter(fitted, residuals, alpha=0.7, edgecolor="k", linewidth=0.3)
axes[0].axhline(0, color="red", linestyle="--")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Fitted values")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Residuals")
axes[0].set_title("Residuals vs Fitted")

# Q-Q plot: points near the line support approximate normality of residuals
sm.qqplot(residuals, line="45", ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("Normal Q-Q Plot of Residuals")

# Observed vs fitted: closeness to diagonal indicates good fit
axes[2].scatter(brain_reg["FSIQ"], fitted, alpha=0.7, edgecolor="k", linewidth=0.3)
lims = [min(brain_reg["FSIQ"].min(), fitted.min()), max(brain_reg["FSIQ"].max(), fitted.max())]
axes[2].plot(lims, lims, "r--")
axes[2].set_xlabel("Observed FSIQ")
axes[2].set_ylabel("Predicted FSIQ")
axes[2].set_title("Observed vs Predicted")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Breusch-Pagan test: null hypothesis = homoscedastic residuals
bp_stat, bp_p, _, _ = het_breuschpagan(residuals, brain_model.model.exog)
print(f"Breusch-Pagan test for heteroscedasticity: stat = {bp_stat:.3f}, p = {bp_p:.4f}")
print("If p is large, we do not reject constant variance; if small, consider robust SEs or transformations.")

<p>Part 1 takeaway: Descriptive tables and plots characterize IQ scores and brain-volume proxies. Welch t-tests (with Mann–Whitney backup) assess gender differences on each measure. The regression quantifies whether MRI_Count remains associated with FSIQ after adjusting for gender; diagnostic plots evaluate whether linear-model assumptions are reasonable for this small sample.</p>
<hr /> <h2 id="Part-2:-1985-CPS-Wages-(CPS_85_Wages.txt)">Part 2: 1985 CPS Wages (CPS_85_Wages.txt)¶</h2><p>Research questions</p>
  • How are hourly wages distributed, and how do wages vary across demographic/employment groups?
  • Which worker characteristics predict log wages after adjustment?
<p>Selected tests and rationale</p> <thead> <th>Analysis</th> <th>Test</th> <th>Why</th> </thead> <tbody> </tbody> <tbody></tbody>
Female vs male wages Welch's t-test on raw wages; coefficient in log model Simple group comparison plus adjusted gap in regression
Union vs non-union Welch's t-test Two independent groups
Occupation categories One-way ANOVA + Kruskal–Wallis Multi-group comparison; non-parametric backup for skewed wages
Wage determinants OLS on log(WAGE) Stabilizes variance; coefficients ≈ proportional changes
Multicollinearity Correlation of AGE vs EXPERIENCE Documented r≈0.98 — include EXPERIENCE, exclude AGE

<h3 id="2.3-Compare-Wages-Between-Groups">2.3 Compare Wages Between Groups¶</h3>
In [22]:
def welch_summary(data, value, group, labels=(0, 1), label_names=("Group0", "Group1")):
    g0 = data.loc[data[group] == labels[0], value]
    g1 = data.loc[data[group] == labels[1], value]
    t, p = stats.ttest_ind(g0, g1, equal_var=False)
    return {
        "comparison": f"{label_names[1]} vs {label_names[0]}",
        f"mean_{label_names[0]}": g0.mean(),
        f"mean_{label_names[1]}": g1.mean(),
        "welch_p": p,
    }

group_comparisons = [
    welch_summary(cps, "WAGE", "SEX", (0, 1), ("Male", "Female")),
    welch_summary(cps, "WAGE", "UNION", (0, 1), ("Non-union", "Union")),
    welch_summary(cps, "WAGE", "SOUTH", (0, 1), ("Non-South", "South")),
]
display(pd.DataFrame(group_comparisons).round(4))

# Multi-group occupation comparison
occ_groups = [cps.loc[cps["OCCUPATION"] == k, "WAGE"].values for k in sorted(cps["OCCUPATION"].unique())]
f_stat, f_p = stats.f_oneway(*occ_groups)
h_stat, h_p = stats.kruskal(*occ_groups)
print(f"Occupation ANOVA: F p-value = {f_p:.4g}")
print(f"Occupation Kruskal-Wallis: p-value = {h_p:.4g}")

<p>Part 2 takeaway: Wages are right-skewed, so log transformation supports regression. Welch tests highlight raw wage gaps by sex, union status, and region; ANOVA/Kruskal–Wallis compare occupations. The multivariable log-wage model reports adjusted associations (including an estimated gender gap) with confidence intervals, p-values, and R²; diagnostic plots assess model adequacy.</p>
<hr /> <h2 id="Part-3:-Iris-Flower-Measurements-(iris.csv)">Part 3: Iris Flower Measurements (iris.csv)¶</h2><p>Research questions</p>
  • How do sepal and petal measurements differ across species?
  • Are observed differences statistically significant after accounting for multiple species?
<p>Selected tests and rationale</p> <thead> <th>Analysis</th> <th>Test</th> <th>Why</th> </thead> <tbody> </tbody> <tbody></tbody>
Species differences (each measurement) One-way ANOVA Standard test for equality of means across 3 groups with balanced n
Non-parametric backup Kruskal–Wallis Distribution-free alternative
Pairwise follow-up Tukey HSD Controls family-wise error rate when ANOVA is significant

anova_rows = []
for col in measurement_cols:
    groups = [iris.loc[iris["species"] == sp, col].values for sp in iris["species"].unique()]
    f_stat, f_p = stats.f_oneway(*groups)
    h_stat, h_p = stats.kruskal(*groups)
    anova_rows.append({
        "measurement": col,
        "anova_F_p": f_p,
        "kruskal_p": h_p,
    })

anova_results = pd.DataFrame(anova_rows)
print("One-way ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis tests (H0: equal distributions/means across species):")
display(anova_results.round(6))

print(
    "\nVery small p-values indicate strong evidence that at least one species differs "
    "from the others for that measurement."
)

<h3 id="3.4-Plain-Language-Summary">3.4 Plain-Language Summary¶</h3><p>The iris dataset contains four flower measurements for three species (setosa, versicolor, virginica), with 50 flowers per species.</p>
  • Sepal variables differ across species, but distributions overlap more than petal variables do.
  • Petal length and petal width show the clearest separation: setosa has small petals, while versicolor and virginica have larger petals, with virginica tending to be largest.
  • One-way ANOVA confirms that mean measurements are not equal across species (very small p-values for all four variables). Tukey follow-up tests identify which species pairs differ.
  • In practice, petal measurements alone could often distinguish species, which is why the iris data are commonly used to teach classification — but here we focus on classical group comparisons and visualization.
<hr /> <h2 id="Conclusion">Conclusion¶</h2><p>This notebook walked through three complementary workflows:</p>
  1. Brain size: descriptive exploration, gender comparisons with Welch/Mann–Whitney tests, and an adjusted linear model relating FSIQ to MRI_Count with assumption diagnostics.
  2. CPS wages: data cleaning, skewed wage distributions, group comparisons, and a log-wage regression interpreting coefficients as approximate percentage effects.
  3. Iris: multi-group ANOVA/Kruskal–Wallis testing and visual evidence of species separation.
<p>Together, these analyses illustrate how to choose tests based on the number of groups, distribution shape, and modeling goals — and how to validate regression assumptions before drawing conclusions.</p>
